section.title: Let Us Go to the House of the Lord
section.sectionRationale: A Song of Ascents of David, third in the pilgrim collection Psalms 120 to 134, placed in Book V of the Psalter, Psalms 107 to 150. Where Psalm 120 cried from a distance and Psalm 121 promised help on the road, this psalm arrives: feet finally standing within Jerusalem's gates.
section.thesis: The joy of arriving at the house of the LORD in a city built for unity and justice moves the pilgrim to pray earnestly for Jerusalem's peace, a joy and a prayer fulfilled in Christ and the heavenly Jerusalem to come.
section.frameNote: Three movements: joyful arrival at Jerusalem's gates, verses 1 to 2, praise for the city's unity and justice, verses 3 to 5, and the call to pray for her peace, verses 6 to 9.

units.label: I was glad when they said to me

verses.text: I was glad when they said to me, "Let us go to the house of the LORD."
Our feet are standing in your gates, O Jerusalem.
Jerusalem is built up as a city united together,
where the tribes go up, the tribes of the LORD, as a testimony for Israel, to give thanks to the name of the LORD.
For there the thrones of judgment stand, the thrones of the house of David.

units.label: Pray for the peace of Jerusalem

verses.text: Pray for the {{shalom|peace}} of Jerusalem: "May those who love you prosper.
May there be peace within your walls, and prosperity inside your fortresses."
For the sake of my brothers and friends, I will say, "Peace be within you."
For the sake of the house of the LORD our God, I will seek your prosperity.

shalom.gloss: Peace, wholeness, security, and prosperity together. Jerusalem's very name plays on this word, so praying for the city's shalom is praying that it live up to its own name.

basic.context: Attributed to David, this Song of Ascents captures the pilgrim's joy at finally arriving in Jerusalem, standing within its gates after the anxious distance of Psalm 120 and the promised help of Psalm 121, and moves from personal gladness to a prayer for the whole city's peace.
basic.hermeneutics: It describes a specific pilgrim's arrival at Jerusalem's gates for worship, and it prescribes as an abiding pattern rejoicing in corporate worship and praying earnestly for the peace of God's city and people.
basic.originalLanguages: The psalmist prays for Jerusalem's shalom, a peace that means wholeness, security, and prosperity together, not merely an absence of war, playing on the city's own name which contains the same root.
basic.typology: The thrones of the house of David set for judgment anticipate the greater Son of David who judges in righteousness, and the joy of going up to the house of the LORD anticipates the joy of believers gathering as living stones in Christ's spiritual temple.
basic.christ: Jesus wept over Jerusalem's failure to know the things that make for peace, Luke 19:41-44, the very peace this psalm prays for, and He is Himself the greater Son of David whose throne of judgment will never fail.
basic.god: God dwells among His gathered people in the city He chose, receiving their thanks and establishing just rule there through the house of David, and He hears the prayers offered for that city's peace.
basic.crossReferences: Luke 19:41-44 shows Jesus weeping over Jerusalem's unrecognized peace. Hebrews 12:22 pictures believers as having come to the heavenly Jerusalem. Revelation 21:2 shows the new Jerusalem descending as the final fulfillment of this psalm's joy and peace.
basic.oneStory: This psalm's joy at arriving in Jerusalem to worship, and its prayer for the city's peace, are fulfilled in Christ and the heavenly Jerusalem, the true and lasting city of peace He is building for His people.

context.literary:
Psalm 122 is built on a movement of feet and a movement of speech. It begins with other people speaking, 'Let us go to the house of the LORD,' verse 1, and it ends with the pilgrim himself speaking, 'Peace be within you,' verse 8, and 'I will seek your prosperity,' verse 9. In between, the poem climbs from the gates of verse 2 to the city's design in verse 3, to the tribes streaming in and the thrones of justice in verses 4 and 5, and then turns outward into a prayer in verses 6 to 9.

Two threads run the length of the psalm. The first is the name Jerusalem, which is spoken in verse 2, verse 3 and verse 6 and is then addressed directly as 'you' and 'your' through verse 9. The city stops being an object of description and becomes a person spoken to. The second thread is the sound of peace. The prayer of verse 6 asks for shalom, verse 7 asks for a different but neighbouring word, shalvah, a settled ease, and verse 8 gives the blessing back as 'Peace be within you.' The ear catches that sound in the very name of the city.

Verse 3 is the hinge. The city is 'built up as a city united together,' and the verb behind 'united' comes from the Hebrew root for joining and for companionship, the root that gives the ordinary word for a friend. The next verse shows what the joining means in practice: separate tribes, 'the tribes of the LORD,' go up as one body.

The poem also keeps a deliberate balance between house and throne. Verse 4 gives the house of worship, 'to give thanks to the name of the LORD,' and verse 5 gives the house of government, 'the thrones of the house of David.' Verse 9 then folds both into one motive, 'the house of the LORD our God.' Worship and justice are never set against each other. Both are reasons to love the city. Among the fifteen Songs of Ascents, this is the psalm that actually arrives. Psalm 120 was far away, Psalm 121 was on the road, and Psalm 122 has its feet inside the gates.
context.historical:
The Songs of Ascents, Psalms 120 to 134, were sung by pilgrims on the climb to Jerusalem, which sits on high ground in the Judean hills, so that 'going up' was both a matter of geography and the ordinary Hebrew idiom for travelling to the sanctuary. The law required every man to appear before the LORD 'in the place He will choose,' three times a year, at the Feast of Unleavened Bread, the Feast of Weeks and the Feast of Tabernacles, Deuteronomy 16:16. A pilgrim arriving for one of those feasts is the natural voice behind 'Our feet are standing in your gates.'

The psalm is headed 'of David,' and the details fit that world well. David captured the fortress of Zion and made it the City of David, 2 Samuel 5:7, and then brought the ark of God up into it with rejoicing, 2 Samuel 6:12 to 17. After that, Jerusalem held both the seat of worship and the throne. The 'thrones of judgment' of verse 5 are the courts of the king, where Israelites came with their grievances, as 2 Samuel 15:2 shows when Absalom intercepted people on their way to the king for a decision. Under Solomon the hall for the throne was called the Hall of Justice, 1 Kings 7:7. The people who sang verse 5 knew that the king's chair was meant to be a place where wrongs were put right.

The phrase 'house of the LORD' does not have to mean Solomon's temple. It was already in use of the sanctuary at Shiloh, 1 Samuel 1:7, so the words do not settle a date by themselves. Some scholars place the psalm in the monarchy, and others think the Songs of Ascents were gathered and shaped for pilgrims after the exile, when 'the tribes' were a memory the returned community held on to. Either way, the people who sang it lived with real threats, which is why verse 7 prays for 'peace within your walls' and 'inside your fortresses.' The walls and citadels were real, and so was the fear that they might be tested. The pilgrim's gladness is the gladness of someone who knows what the city is for and what it costs to keep it.
context.canonical:
Within the Songs of Ascents, Psalm 122 answers the cry of Psalm 120, where the singer lived 'among those who hate peace,' Psalm 120:6, and said, 'I am in favor of peace; but when I speak, they want war,' Psalm 120:7. Psalm 122 is the place where peace is finally the subject of prayer rather than the thing that is missing. It also leans forward into Psalm 128:5, 'May the LORD bless you from Zion, that you may see the prosperity of Jerusalem all the days of your life,' and Psalm 133:1, 'Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers live together in harmony!' Those are the same joys of togetherness that verses 3 and 4 admire.

The Psalter praises Jerusalem in several voices. Psalm 48:12 to 13 invites people to walk round the city, count her towers and tell the next generation. Psalm 87:2 to 3 says that the LORD loves the gates of Zion more than all the dwellings of Jacob. Psalm 132:13 to 14 says that the LORD has chosen Zion and desires it as His home. Psalm 137:5 to 6 turns the love of the city into an oath made in exile. The prophets then carry the vision forward. Isaiah 2:3 sees many peoples saying, 'Come, let us go up to the mountain of the LORD,' which is nearly the exact invitation of Psalm 122:1 spoken by the nations. Zechariah 8:3 promises that Jerusalem will be called the City of Truth.

The New Testament tells the story in two directions. Jesus wept over the city and warned that its house would be left desolate, Matthew 23:37 to 38, yet the crowds also received Him with 'Peace in heaven and glory in the highest,' Luke 19:38. Hebrews 12:22 says believers have 'come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem,' and Revelation 21:2 pictures the new Jerusalem 'coming down out of heaven from God.' Galatians 4:26 calls the Jerusalem above 'our mother.' The pilgrim's gladness is never abolished. It is transferred to a better city.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalmist meant his hearers to feel what it is to belong to a place that belongs to God. Verse 1 treats the call to worship as good news, not as a duty to be endured, and the first lesson is that gladness at the prospect of meeting God together is a proper religious emotion. The invitation arrives from others, so joy is shown to be contagious. It is passed on through a community before it is felt by one person.

He also meant them to see why the city mattered. It is not important because of its stones. Verses 3 to 5 give three reasons: it holds the scattered tribes together, it is where the LORD's name is thanked, and it is where justice is done in the king's court. A city like that is worth praying for. The prayer of verses 6 to 9 is therefore not a political slogan. It is the response of someone who has seen what God has put in the city.

Finally, he meant them to learn that love for God's people is shown in speech. 'For the sake of my brothers and friends, I will say, Peace be within you,' verse 8. The pilgrim does not merely feel peaceful. He decides to say it, and then to act: 'I will seek your prosperity,' verse 9. Prayer here ends in effort. Anyone who has said 'Pray for the peace of Jerusalem' and then walked away was meant to hear a command to bless, and to go on seeking the good of the place, the people and the worship.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Verse 6 is the only imperative in the psalm, 'Pray for the peace of Jerusalem.' Everything else is report: a pilgrim was glad, feet stood in the gates, the tribes go up, the thrones stand. The report is not a command to travel to Jerusalem three times a year. That requirement belonged to the covenant structure of Israel, Deuteronomy 16:16, and Jesus told the Samaritan woman that a time was coming when people would worship the Father 'neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem,' John 4:21, because true worshippers would worship 'in spirit and in truth,' John 4:23. The Christian has no obligation to pilgrimage, and the sanctuary is no longer a building in one place, Revelation 21:22.

What carries over is the pattern of the pilgrim's heart. Gladness at the call to gather, delight in the unity of God's people, a hunger for justice, and a settled habit of blessing the community by name all belong to the church. Believers can still say 'Peace be within you' over a congregation and mean it. The prayer for the earthly city is a fair application too, since Jeremiah told exiles in Babylon to 'seek the prosperity of the city to which I have sent you,' Jeremiah 29:7. The text does not tell Christians how to read current politics in the Middle East, and it is a mistake to take verse 6 as a blank cheque for a particular policy.

debates.question: Does 'the peace of Jerusalem' in verse 6 point only to the earthly city or beyond it?

views.label: Primarily the historic, earthly city of Jerusalem
views.case: The psalm's concrete details, gates, walls, fortresses, and the thrones of David's house, describe a real, physical city under real threat and in need of real peace.

views.label: A pattern fulfilled ultimately in the heavenly Jerusalem
views.case: Hebrews 12:22 and Revelation 21 take up Jerusalem as the pattern for God's final dwelling with His people, suggesting the psalm's prayer finds its complete answer beyond the earthly city.

debates.bearing: Christians rightly pray for the peace of the earthly city while recognizing that the psalm's deepest longing is answered in the peace Christ brings and the heavenly Jerusalem still to come.

debates.question: What does it mean that Jerusalem is 'a city united together' in verse 3?

views.label: A compact, tightly built city
views.case: The verb comes from the root for joining, and ancient Jerusalem was a crowded hill city whose houses and walls were packed close together. On this reading the poet admires how the city is fitted together, and the picture is architectural.

views.label: A city that unites the people
views.case: The next verse speaks of the tribes going up together, and Psalm 133:1 praises brothers who live in harmony. On this reading the joining is social: Jerusalem gathers the scattered tribes into one worshipping body.

debates.bearing: The two readings fit together, because the poet admires a city whose stones and whose people are alike held together. For the church the lesson is the same either way, that the place where God is worshipped should show a visible unity.

debates.question: When was the psalm composed, and does 'of David' mean Davidic authorship?

views.label: Written by David or in his time
views.case: The heading names David, the psalm presupposes the king's throne of judgment, and the city had just become the home of the ark, 2 Samuel 6:12 to 17. 'House of the LORD' was already used of the sanctuary at Shiloh, 1 Samuel 1:7, so the phrase does not require Solomon's temple.

views.label: Written or reshaped for later pilgrims
views.case: The Songs of Ascents were collected as a set, and verse 4 uses the short relative particle she, which is common in later Hebrew though it is not limited to it. The heading could mean 'for David' or 'in David's tradition.'

debates.bearing: The date does not change the psalm's message. Whoever wrote it, Israel sang it as the voice of every pilgrim, and the heading ties the city's joy to the line of David, which is the line that leads to Christ.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 says, in the Hebrew, that the psalmist was glad 'in those who said to me,' and the speakers are plural. Gladness is set off by other people's invitation, and the plain verb samach, 'to rejoice,' is the usual word for festival joy, as in Deuteronomy 16:14. Verse 2 then pairs a participle, 'standing,' with a form of the verb 'to be,' which gives the sense that the pilgrims' feet have been standing in the gates, the journey behind them and the arrival still fresh. The gates are named in the plural, and the city is addressed by name, a way of speaking that treats Jerusalem almost as a host being greeted.

The verb in verse 3 is chavar, 'to join,' in a form that means 'joined, bound together.' The same root gives the ordinary Hebrew word chaver, a companion. The adverb at the end of the verse, yachdav, 'together,' has the same idea of oneness, and it appears in Psalm 133:1 where brothers dwell together. The Hebrew therefore says more than 'a compact city.' It says a city that has been made a companion to itself, an image of fellowship rather than of geometry.

In verse 4 the tribes are called shivte Yah, 'tribes of Yah,' with the short form of the divine name that is heard at the end of hallelujah. The word for tribe here, shevet, also means rod or staff and, by extension, the sceptre of a ruler. A listener from the same song collection hears it again in Psalm 125:3, where 'the scepter of the wicked' is the same word. The tribes are God's rod, and the scepter of the wicked is a counterfeit. The next phrase, edut leYisrael, is rendered 'a testimony for Israel,' from the root that gives the ark of 'the Testimony,' Exodus 25:22. The pilgrimage is itself a witness that this people belong to the LORD.

Verse 6 is built on a play the English cannot carry. The Hebrew begins with a verb that means 'ask,' not 'pray,' sha'alu, 'ask for the shalom of Jerusalem,' and the sound of shalom is heard again in the city's name. Those who love her are to 'prosper,' and the Hebrew verb there carries the thought of ease and quiet. The BSB footnotes record that verse 6 may be 'be secure' and verse 7 may be 'security.' The word in verse 7, shalvah, is a different noun from shalom. It means quiet, ease, an untroubled settledness, as in Proverbs 17:1, 'Better a dry morsel in quietness than a house full of feasting with strife.' Shalom asks for wholeness for the city, and shalvah asks for a rest that is not disturbed.

The last verb, 'I will seek,' is baqash, to seek or search out, with the object tov, 'good.' The Hebrew of verse 9 therefore ends, 'I will seek good for you.' The psalm that began with 'good news' ends with the pilgrim seeking good for his city, and that good is the tov a person works for, not merely hopes to receive.

typology.type: The city where the tribes meet, Psalm 122:3 to 4
typology.fulfillment: Jerusalem is the one place where scattered tribes become one people before the LORD. In the New Testament that gathering is enlarged. Believers 'have come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem,' Hebrews 12:22, and Paul says the Jerusalem above 'is free, and she is our mother,' Galatians 4:26. The Gentiles are 'no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints,' Ephesians 2:19. The type falls short because the earthly city kept divisions inside its walls, and could exclude. The heavenly city is entered only through Christ and has no outsider's court.

typology.type: The thrones of the house of David, Psalm 122:5
typology.fulfillment: David's court was a place where judgment was given and wrongs righted, but the kings often failed, and the throne finally lay empty. The angel told Mary that the Lord God would give her Son 'the throne of His father David,' and that 'His kingdom will never end,' Luke 1:32 to 33. The risen Christ now sits on the Father's throne and promises His people a share in it, Revelation 3:21. Isaiah 9:7 foresaw a reign on David's throne with 'justice and righteousness.' The correspondence is exact, a Davidic king who judges, but Christ's throne does not pass to a successor and cannot be corrupted.

typology.type: The pilgrim going up, Psalm 122:1 to 2
typology.fulfillment: Israel's pilgrim went up to Jerusalem to appear before God. Jesus Himself made that journey as a boy, Luke 2:41 to 42, and with settled determination at the end of His ministry, 'Jesus resolutely set out for Jerusalem,' Luke 9:51. He arrived there as the true meeting place of God and humankind. When He said, 'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up again,' He was speaking 'about the temple of His body,' John 2:19 to 21. After Him believers 'like living stones, are being built into a spiritual house,' 1 Peter 2:5. The type falls short in that the pilgrimage was a periodic visit, while in Christ God's people live permanently in His presence.

typology.type: Peace within the walls, Psalm 122:6 to 8
typology.fulfillment: The prayer for peace within Jerusalem's walls finds its answer in the person who 'Himself is our peace, who has made the two one and has torn down the dividing wall of hostility,' Ephesians 2:14. Where the psalm asks for peace around the city, Christ builds a people in whom 'the whole building is fitted together and grows into a holy temple,' Ephesians 2:21. The correspondence is real, since the psalm longed for unity and safety. It falls short in that the psalm's peace was bounded by walls and fortresses, and its guarantee could be undone, while Christ's peace is established by His blood and held by Him.

study.christ:
Jesus belongs inside this psalm before He is its fulfilment, because He was one of its pilgrims. The Gospels record that He went up to Jerusalem for the feasts, Luke 2:41 to 42, and that the final approach of His ministry was a pilgrim's march with a purpose that no other pilgrim had, Luke 9:51. When the crowds greeted Him, 'Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!' Luke 19:38, they used the language of the pilgrim psalms, and this psalm in particular, which pairs the name of the LORD with a prayer for peace.

The tragedy of the triumphal entry is that the city prayed for its peace and missed the One who brings it. Luke gives His words as He came near: 'If only you had known on this day what would bring you peace!' Luke 19:42. The psalm's central word, peace, is the very thing He came to bring, and the city that sang for it did not recognise it when it came. His sorrow shows His love for the place the psalm loves, and His lament, 'how often I have longed to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings,' Matthew 23:37, answers the psalm's picture of a city 'united together.' The gathering the psalmist praised was what the Lord wanted, and it was refused.

The psalm's thrones belong to Him. The house of David was to be the place of judgment, and Jesus is the Son of David whose throne has no end, Luke 1:32 to 33. His rule is the one under which 'justice and righteousness' are established, Isaiah 9:7. He is also the replacement of the house. His body is the temple, John 2:21, so that the 'house of the LORD' that the psalmist loved is now found where Christ is found. Believers who gather to worship are 'built together into a dwelling place for God in His Spirit,' Ephesians 2:22.

Paul says that He 'Himself is our peace,' Ephesians 2:14, and that He has 'made the two one.' The Hebrew shalom that the pilgrim asks of the city is a person. A reading that says every detail is a coded reference to Jesus should be resisted, and the gates, the walls and the fortresses need no spiritual translation. The connections that stand are those the New Testament makes, that He is the king on David's throne, the true temple, and the source of the peace the pilgrim asked for.
study.god:
The first thing the psalm shows about God is that He is a God who has a house and a people. The pilgrim is glad to go to 'the house of the LORD,' and the city is full of 'the tribes of the LORD.' The LORD does not stay remote from His people. He has chosen to settle among them, Psalm 132:13 to 14, so that the people can find Him in a place and meet Him there, Exodus 25:22. The psalm does not claim that heaven and earth cannot contain Him. Solomon prayed that His eyes would be open toward the temple, 'the place of which You said, My Name shall be there,' 1 Kings 8:29. The God of this psalm is both enthroned in heaven and attentive on earth.

He is a God of order and justice. The thrones of verse 5 are 'thrones of judgment,' and the psalm counts them among the glories of Jerusalem. That tells us that He does not treat worship and justice as separate parts of religion. The king's court belongs beside the sanctuary because the God who is thanked is the God who rules. The same God who is praised 'to give thanks to the name of the LORD,' verse 4, is the one who sets the king to judge fairly.

He is also a God who unites. The tribes were scattered across the land, and they were different in character and region. He draws them to one place and makes them one people. The word 'united' in verse 3 is a gift God gives as much as a state He observes. Behind it is His covenant promise that He would have a people, and His commitment to gather them.

He gives peace, and He is addressed in the peace that the psalm prays for. The prayer 'May there be peace within your walls' is addressed to the city, but the one who answers prayer is the LORD. The call to 'pray' means that peace is something God gives in answer, and that people cannot produce it simply by effort. At the same time, 'I will seek your prosperity' shows that God works through those who pray.

For worship, the psalm teaches that gladness is a fitting response to being invited to meet God. It teaches that praying for a community is part of loving God. It also teaches humility, since a city that is 'built' and 'united' is held together by the one who chose it. The LORD of this psalm is not a distant power. He is a God who joins people together under His name, and who hears the prayer of someone who wants good for His house.

crossReferences.note: The opening of the Songs of Ascents has the singer living far from home among people who hate peace and want war. Psalm 122 is the arrival that answers it. The one who said 'I am in favor of peace' in a hostile land now stands inside the gates of the city of peace and prays for it.

The law required all the men to appear before the LORD 'in the place He will choose' three times a year. The pilgrim's gladness is the heart behind that command. What was written as an obligation is sung here as a joy, which shows what the law was meant to produce.

David brought the ark up into the City of David 'with rejoicing,' dancing before the LORD. That event made Jerusalem the home of both the king and the ark, which is why the psalm can speak of the house of the LORD and the house of David in the same breath.

Solomon built a hall for the throne, 'the Hall of Justice, where he was to judge.' It is the architectural form of the 'thrones of judgment' in verse 5, a reminder that the Davidic throne was to be a place where right was done.

This psalm of the same collection praises brothers who live together in harmony. It gives the human side of the 'city united together' of Psalm 122:3. Together they show that the unity pilgrims admire in the city is meant to be lived in the people.

Exiles in Babylon were told to seek the prosperity of the city where God had sent them and to pray for it. The command shows that praying for a city's good was not limited to Jerusalem, and that the pattern of Psalm 122:6 to 9 can be lived out wherever God's people are.

Many peoples say, 'Come, let us go up to the mountain of the LORD,' which is the pilgrim's invitation in Psalm 122:1 spoken by the nations. The gladness of one people's pilgrimage becomes the hope of every people, and the law goes out from Zion to them.

Jesus laments over the city that kills the prophets and stones those sent to her, and He says He longed to gather her children. Psalm 122 sings of a city united and at peace, and the Lord grieves over a city that refuses the gathering He offered, until she says, 'Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord.'

Christ Himself is our peace. He tears down the dividing wall and makes one people from two, fellow citizens in God's household and a holy temple. The things Psalm 122 admires, unity, a dwelling for God and peace within the walls, are found in the church that Christ builds.

Believers 'have come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem.' The pilgrim's arrival at the gates is completed here. The writer says that those who belong to Christ already stand where the psalmist longed to stand.

The holy city, the new Jerusalem, comes down out of heaven from God, adorned like a bride. The city of Psalm 122 is a promise of the city that will finally be at peace, where God dwells with His people and nothing threatens the walls.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 122 sits in the story at the point where God's people have a place. Creation began with a garden where God walked with humanity, and the fall drove the pair out. Everything afterwards is the long work of bringing a people back into God's presence. The tabernacle, then the ark's arrival in the City of David, then Solomon's temple, are stages in that return. Psalm 122 sings the joy of one who stands in the place where the return has reached, 'Our feet are standing in your gates, O Jerusalem.'

The psalm also looks back to what was promised to the patriarchs. God told Abraham that He would make of him a nation and give him a land. Here that promise is seen in one place, with twelve tribes gathered, a king seated and a house for the name. The thrones of judgment answer the lawless days when 'everyone did what was right in his own eyes,' Judges 21:25. It is the first settled order of a kingdom that God rules through a man.

But Jerusalem's peace was repeatedly threatened and eventually broken. The prophets who loved the city also warned that her leaders judged for a bribe and that Zion would be plowed like a field, Micah 3:11 to 12. The Babylonians destroyed the walls the pilgrim prayed over, and the exiles swore never to forget her, Psalm 137:5 to 6. The song of arrival could be sung again only because God promised to return to Zion and dwell in Jerusalem, Zechariah 8:3. Even then the city did not know the things that make for peace, and Jesus wept.

The story reaches its answer in Christ. He is the king whose throne is for ever, the temple raised in three days, and the peace Himself. The church is the people He gathers from every nation, a city 'united together' by His Spirit. The one story ends with the vision of Revelation 21, 'the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God,' and a city with no temple 'because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple,' Revelation 21:22. The pilgrim who was glad to be told 'Let us go to the house of the LORD' will find that the house has come to live among those who were invited to it, and the peace he prayed for will have no end.

sermon.title: A Pilgrim's Journey
sermon.why: Begg treats Psalms 120 to 122 together as one pilgrim's journey, showing how the ascent moves from distress, through promised help, to the joy of arrival at Jerusalem's gates and the call to pray for the city's peace.

quiz.q: What made the psalmist glad, according to verse 1?

options.text: Others inviting him, 'Let us go to the house of the LORD.'
options.note: This is the exact occasion for his gladness, stated at the outset.
The gladness is tied to corporate worship, not material gain.
The psalm's joy is about worship and arrival, not conquest.
Harvest joy appears in other psalms, such as 126, not the stated cause here.

quiz.q: What is said to make Jerusalem strong, according to verse 3?

options.text: It is built up as a city united together.
options.note: This unity, not walls alone, is what the psalm highlights.

options.text: Its vast size compared to other cities.
options.note: The psalm emphasizes unity, not sheer size.
Trade is not mentioned; the emphasis is on unity and worship.
The text speaks of internal unity, not geographic isolation.

quiz.q: What stands in Jerusalem according to verse 5?

options.text: Thrones of judgment, the thrones of the house of David.
options.note: This roots the city's justice in the Davidic line.
The verse names thrones of righteous judgment tied to David, not idolatry.
The psalm does not mention commerce here.
Walls are mentioned later, in verse 7, but verse 5 specifically names thrones of judgment.

quiz.q: What does the psalmist urge people to do for Jerusalem in verse 6?

options.note: This direct exhortation opens the psalm's closing section.
The psalm calls for engaged prayer, not avoidance.
The concern here is prayer for peace, not a building project.

options.text: Pay increased taxes to the king.
options.note: Taxation is not the subject; prayer for peace is.

quiz.q: How does this psalm's vision of Jerusalem connect to the New Testament?

options.text: It anticipates the heavenly Jerusalem and Christ, the greater Son of David whose throne endures forever.
options.note: Hebrews 12:22 and Luke 1:32-33 show this fulfillment.

options.text: It has no connection beyond ancient Israelite history.
options.note: The New Testament directly takes up both the Davidic throne and the Jerusalem imagery.

options.text: It predicts the exact date of Jerusalem's fall in AD 70.
options.note: The psalm's focus is on typology and hope, not a specific date.

options.text: It shows Jesus rejecting Jerusalem entirely.
options.note: Jesus weeps over the city out of love, longing for its peace, not rejection of it.

questions: The psalmist was glad simply at the invitation to worship together. What is your own posture toward gathering with God's people, eager or reluctant?
Jerusalem's strength is described as unity, not merely walls. Where is disunity weakening the church or community you belong to?
The psalm ties Jerusalem's justice to David's throne. How does trusting Christ, the greater Son of David, shape how you respond to injustice you witness or experience?
The psalmist prays for Jerusalem's peace for the sake of brothers, friends, and the house of the LORD. Who and what are you actively praying for the peace and good of right now?

This psalm's joy and prayer find their fullest answer in the heavenly Jerusalem still to come. How does that future hope shape your patience with the imperfect gatherings and cities you belong to today?

translationNotes.note: The invitation 'Let us go to the house of the LORD' reflects the communal nature of pilgrimage, worship undertaken together rather than alone.
Built up as a city united together can also be rendered compact or tightly joined, an image drawn from Jerusalem's dense architecture as well as its social and covenantal unity.
Pray for the peace of Jerusalem contains a wordplay in Hebrew between Jerusalem and shalom, peace, so the prayer is in effect that the city live up to its own name.
